name: ConsentX — Cookie Consent & Compliance
author: ConsentX

sections.description:
ConsentX is a complete consent-management platform for WordPress, and the WordPress client for the ConsentX service.

You need a free ConsentX account, and connecting takes one email address. Install the plugin, open ConsentX → Settings, type your email and press Connect my site: ConsentX creates the account, registers this domain and sends back the site key that links the two. The banner goes live at that moment — before it, the plugin adds nothing to your pages. That is deliberate rather than a paywall. A banner on its own collects a decision and keeps it in the visitor’s own browser, where you cannot produce it for anyone who asks; the account is what turns a dialog into a record you hold.

Unlike a thin “loader” plugin, the banner, the script blocking and Google Consent Mode then run inside WordPress and are served from your own domain, so a slow or blocked CDN cannot take your consent notice off your site. The hosted ConsentX widget is there as an option if you would rather manage every site from one dashboard.

Free, once connected:

  • Consent banner — nine layouts and six colour schemes, picked from live previews; a full preference center with per-category toggles; and a floating “manage consent” button.
  • Automatic script blocking — third-party scripts, pixels and iframes are held before consent and released the moment the visitor accepts, using a client-side blocker (createElement guard + MutationObserver) plus optional blocking of your own enqueued handles.
  • Blocked-content placeholders — blocked YouTube/Maps/embeds become tidy “click to accept” boxes with per-service consent.
  • Google Consent Mode v2 — denied-by-default signals set before any tag, updated automatically on the visitor’s choice. Cache-safe (no consent state baked into cached HTML).
  • Region-aware consent — opt-in (GDPR/UK/EU/LGPD/POPIA/DPDPA) vs opt-out (US/CCPA/Canada/Australia) resolved per visitor.
  • The same banner everywhere — Classic Bar, Floating Card, Brand Dock, Center Modal, Corner Toast, Top Slim Bar, Bottom Sheet, Liquid Glass and Preference Center, in Light, Dark, Midnight, Sand, Forest or High contrast. The same nine shapes and six schemes ConsentX offers on Wix, Shopify and Webflow, so one brand looks like one brand.
  • Cookie-policy generator — generate a Cookie Policy (and Privacy Statement) with a live cookie table, plus [consentx-cookies], [consentx-manage-consent] and [consentx-revoke-link] shortcodes.
  • Proof of consent — immutable, timestamped snapshots of exactly what you asked visitors to consent to for each policy version.
  • Accessibility — focus-trapped dialogs, ARIA roles, keyboard support, and reduced-motion respect.

What the account adds beyond the banner:

  • Consent receipts stored in your ConsentX dashboard — the record that proves a choice was made, exportable for an audit.
  • Cloud cookie scanning synced into your local cookie list.
  • Cross-site and multisite management, DSAR workflow and compliance reports.

Connecting takes one email address, typed into ConsentX → Settings. If you already have a ConsentX site key, you can paste that instead. Nothing is sent to ConsentX until you press the button.

External services

This plugin can connect to ConsentX (https://consentx.io), the service this plugin is the
WordPress client for. What is sent, and when:

Before you connect — nothing leaves your site, and nothing is added to it: no banner, no
script blocking, no Consent Mode signal. One exception, in wp-admin only: opening the
ConsentX → Plans screen fetches the public price list from
https://app.consentx.io/api/public/plans. That request is anonymous – it carries no site
address, no account and no visitor data – and the result is cached. Nothing is sent from the
front end of your site, and nothing is sent about your visitors.

When you press “Connect my site” and give an email address — and only then — your server
posts that email, this site’s domain, its name, a one-time code, and this install’s banner
settings (its layout, colour scheme and the two lines of copy) and the names of its consent
categories, to https://app.consentx.io/api/public/sites/claim. The banner and category
details are what let your ConsentX dashboard show your own banner rather than a stock one;
they describe your configuration, not your visitors. ConsentX then makes one request back to this
site, to /wp-json/consentx/v1/verify, to check the code is really being served here: that is
what stops anyone from registering a domain they do not run. If the email is new, a ConsentX
account is created for it and you are emailed a link to set a password; if it already exists,
this site is added to it and the account holder is emailed to say so. What comes back is a site
key and an API token, which are stored in your WordPress options table. Nothing here happens on
activation, on a page load, or on any schedule – only when an administrator fills in that form.

After your site is linked, by that form or by pasting a site key into ConsentX → Settings,
these requests begin:

  • Your server asks https://app.consentx.io/api/v1/me, /api/v1/cookies and /api/v1/consents
    for your account, your scanned cookie list and your stored consent records. These carry a
    scoped API token as an Authorization: Bearer header – a separate secret from the site key,
    issued to your account and stored only in your WordPress options table. Without that token
    these requests are never made.
  • If “push consent receipts” is on, a visitor’s browser posts their consent choice to
    https://app.consentx.io/api/ when they accept or reject: the categories they
    chose, the time, the policy version, and the data your ConsentX dashboard shows as a consent
    receipt. This is the record that proves consent was given, which is the reason the service
    exists. Turn it off in ConsentX → Settings and consent is stored only in the visitor’s browser.
  • If you switch rendering to “hosted”, the banner script is loaded from
    https://app.consentx.io/api//embed.js instead of from this plugin. Local
    rendering is the default and keeps all code inside WordPress.

The banner self-check is not an external request: it asks YOUR site for YOUR home page
(https://your-site/?consentx-selfcheck=…) and reads the HTML locally. Nothing about the
check, and nothing from the page, is sent to ConsentX.

Region detection never leaves your site: it reads the geo headers your own CDN or host already
sets, through this plugin’s own REST route. No visitor IP address is sent to ConsentX by this
plugin.

ConsentX terms of service: https://app.consentx.io/terms
ConsentX privacy policy: https://app.consentx.io/privacy
sections.installation:
1. Upload the consentx folder to /wp-content/plugins/, or install the ZIP via Plugins → Add New → Upload.
  2. Activate the plugin. Nothing is added to your site yet, and nothing is sent anywhere.
  3. Open ConsentX → Overview and pick a layout and colour scheme from the live previews.
  4. Type your email address in the card at the top of ConsentX → Overview — the screen activation opens — and press Connect my site. ConsentX creates your account, registers this domain and returns a site key: your banner is live from that moment, and every consent decision is recorded against your site. Check your email for a link to set a password.
  5. The screen then says Website connected, and checks your banner for you: it fetches your own home page the way a visitor would and tells you whether the banner is in it. Press Check my banner any time to run that again — after clearing a cache, for instance.
sections.faq:
Do I need a ConsentX account?

Yes, and it is free. The plugin is the WordPress client for the ConsentX service: it shows no banner, blocks no scripts and emits no Consent Mode signals until this site is connected. Connecting is one email address on the Settings screen – no dashboard visit, no key to copy. Without it the plugin could collect a decision but not keep a record of it, which is the part a regulator asks for.

I was already using the plugin without an account. Does this update switch my banner off?

No. An install that was already showing a banner keeps showing it, and nothing on your site changes. The Settings screen will explain what connecting adds – chiefly a stored record of what your visitors chose, which a banner on its own cannot keep.

How do I know the banner is really live?

The plugin checks for you. After connecting – and whenever you press Check my banner on the Overview screen – it requests your own home page the way a visitor would, with no admin session, and looks for the banner in the HTML that comes back. If your home page loads but the banner is not in it, you are told that, with the usual cause (a page cache built before you connected). If your host blocks a server from fetching itself, you are told the check could not run – which is not the same as a broken banner, and is not reported as one.

Where is the banner’s code served from?

From your own domain, by default. The plugin renders the banner, runs the blocker and drives Consent Mode inside WordPress; only consent records travel to ConsentX. If you would rather ConsentX served the banner itself – the same embed script it gives a site with no WordPress behind it, managed from your dashboard – switch Rendering mode to “From ConsentX” in Settings.

Does it block scripts automatically?

Yes. Known third-party trackers, pixels and iframes are held before consent and released on acceptance. You can also list your own enqueued script handles to block.

Is it compatible with caching plugins?

Yes. No consent or region state is written into cached HTML — the banner reads consent client-side and resolves region via a lightweight request — and our tags carry optimizer-skip attributes so minify/defer plugins leave them alone.

Does it support Google Consent Mode v2?

Yes, natively and locally: denied-by-default signals are set before any tag and updated on the visitor’s choice.
sections.changelog:
2.9.9

A large release. Everything below is new since 1.0.2, the version most sites
are running; the 2.x work was developed and tested outside this listing, so it
is summarised here rather than listed release by release.

  • New: banner designer. Nine layouts, six colour schemes, your own wording, and a live preview — all inside WordPress.
  • New: cookie scanning. Finds the cookies your site actually sets and keeps your cookie table in step with them.
  • New: consent records. What each visitor chose, when, from which country, and the reference you would quote to a regulator.
  • New: data requests (DSAR), with the statutory deadline shown on each one.
  • New: cookie policy and privacy statement pages, generated and kept current with your cookie list.
  • New: categories and per-category script blocking, including your own enqueued handles.
  • Improved: Google Consent Mode v2 defaults are set before any tag fires, so a visitor’s choice is respected from the first page view.
  • Improved: the banner follows each visitor’s own law automatically — opt-in for the EU and UK, opt-out for the US, strictest model when a location cannot be read.
  • Improved: an installation check that fetches your home page AND the banner script, so “your banner is live” means it is actually serving.
  • Security: all admin actions carry capability and nonce checks; all inline output goes through core’s enqueue and inline-script APIs.

Upgrading from 1.0.2 keeps your connection. Your site key and settings are read
from the same place and nothing on your site changes without you.

1.0.2

  • Fix: the connect callback URL is now built with a raw nonce. wp_nonce_url() HTML-encoded the ampersand (&), which corrupted the _wpnonce parameter on the return trip and failed the security check.

1.0.1

  • Fix: the “Connect to ConsentX” button now reaches the authorize screen. The off-site redirect host is allowlisted (it was being dropped by wp_safe_redirect) and the callback URL is no longer double-encoded.

1.0.0

  • Initial release: 1-click connect, Google Consent Mode v2 defaults, optional pre-consent script blocking, and manual site-key fallback.

short_description: Cookie consent for GDPR, CCPA and DPDPA: banner, script blocking, Google Consent Mode v2, policy pages. Needs a free ConsentX account.
